vt.analysis:
Type: OpenClaw Skill
Name: web-collection
Version: 1.1.9

The skill bundle provides a framework for web data collection with capabilities for local bridge control, cloud API dispatch, and remote execution via SSH. Significant security risks include the use of 'ssh' to execute scripts on remote hosts in 'run.sh' and the execution of arbitrary shell commands via the '--bridge-cmd' flag in 'collect_and_export_loop.sh'. While these features appear aligned with the stated purpose of managing distributed collection connectors, the high-privilege nature of these operations and the handling of user API tokens in 'export_preference.sh' present a significant attack surface for potential abuse or command injection.

llm.summary: The skill's code and instructions generally match a browser-extension collection tool, but several practices (unknown source, instruction to use the user's normal Chrome profile, and storing/using a user API token) pose meaningful privacy/security risks and deserve caution before installation.

dimensions.detail: Name/description, required binaries (curl, node), and the scripts all align with a web/browser-extension collection tool that can run locally or dispatch through a cloud connector. The need for an API token and a cloud base URL is coherent for a cloud-dispatch mode.
dimensions.label: Purpose & Capability
dimensions.name: purpose_capability

dimensions.detail: SKILL.md explicitly instructs using the user's normal Chrome environment (not an isolated profile), and the scripts operate a closed-loop with a local bridge/connector — meaning the skill can cause browser-extension-driven collection of user-visible data. The skill also asks the agent to solicit and persist the user's cloud API token and to run bridge startup commands if requested. These actions can access or transmit sensitive browser/extension data and should be treated as high risk unless the connector and extension are trusted.
dimensions.label: Instruction Scope
dimensions.name: instruction_scope

dimensions.detail: No install spec is provided (instruction-only entrypoint) and the repo ships bash scripts. Nothing in the manifests downloads or executes third-party code at install time. Risk arises at runtime when the scripts call external endpoints or run a user-supplied bridge command.
dimensions.label: Install Mechanism
dimensions.name: install_mechanism

dimensions.detail: The skill does not demand unrelated cloud or system credentials, but it does request and persist a 'defaultCloudToken' (user API token) when cloud mode is used and reads/writes preferences under $OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR or $HOME/.openclaw. Storing the token locally is reasonable for cloud dispatch but is sensitive — the user should understand where that token is stored and who can access the connector endpoint.
dimensions.label: Credentials
dimensions.name: environment_proportionality

dimensions.detail: always:false and autonomous invocation is the platform default. The skill writes only to its own preferences file and does not modify other skills or system-wide settings. It optionally can run an externally supplied bridge command (user-specified) which may spawn other processes — user control is required for that.
dimensions.label: Persistence & Privilege
dimensions.name: persistence_privilege

llm.guidance: This skill implements a browser-extension collection flow and will ask for/optionally persist a cloud API token and preferences under $OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR or $HOME/.openclaw. Before installing: 1) Verify you trust the skill source — this package has no homepage and an unknown origin. 2) Understand that it prefers using your normal Chrome profile (not an isolated profile), which could expose cookies, sessions, or other browser data to the connector/extension — avoid giving it access to your main profile unless you fully trust the extension and connector. 3) If using cloud mode, treat the cloud token like any secret: confirm the target cloud base URL is correct and trusted, and be aware the token will be stored locally (the scripts mask it when showing preferences but persist it in plain JSON). 4) If you enable --ensure-bridge or provide a bridge start command, inspect that command carefully (it will be executed on your machine). 5) Consider running tests in an isolated environment or with a throwaway browser profile and limited credentials first. If you need higher confidence, ask the publisher for provenance, an official homepage, and to explain how the connector/extension protects collected data.
